info.name: user-management-api — REST
info.description:
REST collection for the user-management API. Start the server with `make up`, select the **user-management-api — local** environment, then **just hit Send** — a pre-request script registers, logs in and attaches `Authorization: Bearer …` for you.

Folders are ordered, so the Collection Runner (or `make postman`) can run the lot; folder 5 cleans up so it is re-runnable.

- `POST /auth/register` returns a user but **no token** — a login always follows it.
- No roles: PATCH/DELETE work on your own id only, anything else is `403`.

exec: // Auto-auth. Runs before every request in this collection.
//   1. Seeds a unique set of credentials the first time it runs.
//   2. On any request that needs a token, makes sure a fresh one is stored
//      (logging in, and registering first if that account does not exist yet).
// The Authorization header itself is attached by the collection-level Bearer
// auth (value {{access_token}}); this script only keeps that variable current.
// Write to the active environment when there is one, so the values survive a
// restart and stay out of the committed collection file.
// >= 8 runes and not in the server's common-password blacklist.
// --- 2. make sure we hold a usable access token ---------------------------
// Endpoints that must never be called with a token attached, or that would
// Nothing to do — Postman continues with the request immediately.
console.log('[auto-auth] signed in as ' + data.user.email + ' (' + data.user.id + ')');
jsonPost('/api/v1/auth/login', { email: getVar('email'), password: getVar('password') }, cb);
// No such account yet (401 INVALID_CREDENTIALS) — create it, then log in.
console.error('[auto-auth] register failed — is the server up? ' + regErr);

item.name: 1. Health
item.description: Liveness and readiness. Both are public and answer a flat body, not the `{"data": ...}` envelope.

request.description: Liveness probe. Always 200 while the process is alive.
Readiness probe — pings MongoDB. 503 with `{"status":"unavailable"}` when the database is unreachable, or `{"status":"draining"}` during shutdown.

exec: pm.test('200 OK — MongoDB reachable', function () { pm.response.to.have.status(200); });

item.name: 2. Auth
item.description: Public endpoints. `register` creates the account but returns **no token** — you always log in afterwards. `refresh` rotates: the refresh token you send is revoked and a brand-new pair comes back.

request.description:
Creates a user. `201` with `Location: /api/v1/users/{id}` and `{"data": user}` — no token.

If the account was already created by the auto-auth script (or by a previous run) this answers `409 EMAIL_TAKEN`, which the test accepts as a valid outcome.

exec: pm.test('201 Created, or 409 if the account already exists', function () {
pm.test('never leaks a password field', function () {
pm.test('Location header points at the new user', function () {
pm.test('no token is issued by register', function () {

request.description:
Exchanges email + password for a session. The test script saves `access_token`, `refresh_token`, `token_expires_at` and `user_id`, so every later request is authenticated.

The access token is an HS256 JWT (15m by default); the refresh token is 64 hex characters (168h).

exec: pm.test('access token is a JWT', function () {
pm.test('refresh token is 64 hex characters', function () {

request.description:
Rotates the session. The refresh token you send is revoked immediately and a whole new pair is returned — the saved variables are overwritten with it.

Replaying an already-rotated token is treated as theft: every session of that user is wiped.

exec: pm.test('the refresh token was rotated', function () {
pm.test('a new access token came back', function () {

item.name: 3. Users
item.description: Authenticated endpoints. The `Authorization: Bearer {{access_token}}` header is inherited from the collection — nothing to set by hand.

request.description:
Same body as `register`, but requires a token. Creates a **second** account whose id is saved as `other_user_id` — the 403 test later tries to modify it, which is how the self-only rule is demonstrated.

The email is regenerated on every send, so this never collides.

exec: // Always a fresh address, so re-running never hits EMAIL_TAKEN.

request.description: Default page: `limit=20`. Returns `{"data": [...], "meta": {"limit", "next_cursor", "has_more"}}`.

exec: pm.test('data is an array of users', function () {
pm.test('no password hash anywhere in the payload', function () {

request.description: Keyset pagination, page 1. Saves `meta.next_cursor` into the `next_cursor` variable for the next request.

exec: pm.test('exactly one user came back', function () {

query.description: the next_cursor returned by the previous page

request.description: Page 2, using the cursor saved by the previous request. Feed `meta.next_cursor` back in until `has_more` is false.

query.description: case-insensitive substring of name or email

request.description: `query` is a case-insensitive substring match against name **or** email.

exec: pm.test('every hit actually matches the query', function () {

request.description: Reads one user. `{{user_id}}` is your own id, saved at login. Any authenticated caller may read any user.

exec: pm.test('it is the user we asked for', function () {

request.description:
Partial update. Send only the fields you want changed — `name`, `email`, or both. Omitting a field leaves it untouched; an empty body is `422`.

Only your own id is allowed; see the 403 case in the *Error cases* folder.

exec: pm.test('the email was left untouched', function () {

item.name: 4. Error cases
item.description: Every failure mode the API defines, each asserting the exact `error.code`. Error bodies are `{"error": {"code", "message", "details"}, "request_id"}`.

request.description: Auth is switched off on this request only, so no `Authorization` header is sent. Also checks the `WWW-Authenticate` challenge.

exec: pm.test('the error carries a request_id', function () {

request.description: Unknown email, wrong password and a malformed email all answer the same `401 INVALID_CREDENTIALS` — the API never reveals whether an account exists.

exec: pm.test('does not reveal whether the account exists', function () {

request.description: The only authorization rule in the service: PATCH and DELETE work on your own id only. There are no roles — a second account cannot be edited even by the account that created it.
A well-formed 24-hex ObjectId that no user has.
Registers the address that already belongs to the current session.
Passwords must be at least 8 runes and must not be one of the well-known weak ones (`password`, `12345678`, `p@ssw0rd`, …). Failures come back with a per-field `details` array.

exec: pm.test('details point at the password field', function () {

request.description: `limit` must be an integer in 1..100.

exec: pm.test('code is VALIDATION_ERROR on the limit field', function () {

request.description: Ids must be 24 hex characters. A malformed one is rejected before the database is touched — that is a validation error, not a 404.

exec: pm.test('code is VALIDATION_ERROR on the id field', function () {

request.description: A PATCH has to change something — at least one of `name` or `email`.

exec: pm.test('code is VALIDATION_ERROR on the body', function () {

request.description: Truncated JSON. Decoding fails before validation, so this is `400 MALFORMED_JSON`, not `422`.
Even a route that does not exist answers in the error envelope.
`/auth/login` exists, but only for POST.

exec: pm.test('405 Method Not Allowed', function () { pm.response.to.have.status(405); });

item.name: 5. Cleanup
item.description: Deletes both accounts the run created, so the collection can be run again from scratch. Run this last — deleting your own account invalidates the stored token, and the auto-auth script will simply register again on the next run.

request.description: Self-only deletion means the second account has to delete itself — the pre-request script logs in as it and uses *its* token for this one request.

exec: // Log in as the second account so it can delete itself.
console.error('[cleanup] could not sign in as the second account');

request.description:
`204 No Content`. Deleting a user also revokes every refresh token they hold.

The test then clears the stored session, so the next run of the collection registers a fresh account instead of trying to use a token for a user that no longer exists.

exec: // Reset the session so a re-run starts clean.
